body.text: MP calls for nuclear moratorium to be lifted after success of Australian-made reactor
In short:
A central Queensland MP wants the nuclear energy moratorium lifted following the success of an Australian founder's microreactor.
Renewable energy advocates have warned against the high costs and lack of community support for nuclear in Australia.
What's next?
The federal minister for energy has ruled out nuclear power, describing it as a "pipe dream".
Travelling along country roads from Texas to Idaho in the United States, an Australian-owned company is transporting an unconventional load: a nuclear reactor that fits in the back of a ute.

The microreactor was developed by Deployable Energy under a US government pilot program, set up in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump to accelerate the production of new advanced reactors.
Owned by Brisbane-raised Bobby Gallagher, the company was able to make a microreactor that reached criticality in 155 days.
Criticality is a key step towards commercialisation in which a reactor achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.
The microreactor promises to deliver 3.5 megawatts of thermal power and can be adapted to nautical environments.

"It provides electrical power to power up to 1,000 homes for five years without needing to be refuelled and then it can just be swapped out after that five-year period … like a gas bottle," Mr Gallagher said.
Mr Gallagher's company is conducting safety testing at the Idaho National Laboratory, with the aim of producing 1,000 units per year from its manufacturing facility in Texas by 2030.
He said it could help power remote communities, islands, mine sites, manufacturing industries and data centres.
"The potential is to be able to provide affordable, modular, scalable power to where it's needed in Australia without the constraints of the grid or traditional infrastructure,"
Mr Gallagher said.
It has caught the attention of the federal LNP member for Flynn, Colin Boyce, who has renewed his calls for Australia to lift its moratorium on nuclear energy.
"[For] the future of the Australian energy map, we need to explore all options and have all options available to business and industry," he said.

"The greatest tragedy of that nuclear moratorium in Australia is that we've lost a generation of young people in our education system who have not pursued nuclear engineering or nuclear medicine or nuclear chemistry.
"We have literally got dozens and dozens and dozens of people who are now overseas learning about nuclear."
Social licence

The Coalition took a controversial policy to the 2025 federal election to replace seven aging coal-fired power stations with nuclear reactors, including the Callide Power Station in Mr Boyce's central Queensland electorate.
Mr Boyce did not support the policy but said he had had a positive reception from his constituents about exploring nuclear as an energy option.
Coordinator of the Gladstone Conservation Council Emma Smith said she was apprehensive about hosting nuclear in her backyard, and that it was not the "right solution" for the region.
"Central Queensland is really interesting in that we're quite used to new projects and we're used to being quite relatively close to power generation," she said.
"We need to be working towards things that will meet our needs now, which is building the renewable energy that we have."

The head of research at pro-renewables organisation Rewiring Australia, Calum Harvey-Scholes, said while the cost of living remained a concern for energy consumers, he could not imagine widespread public support for nuclear.
"I think getting people to a place where they're happy to have [nuclear energy] in their community or on their doorstep is hard to imagine," he said.
"It's going to take a huge amount of work for a technology that we just don't need."
Mr Harvey-Scholes also questioned whether building nuclear energy in Australia would bring down energy bills.
"Batteries are bringing that kind of reliability, that people were worried about with solar and wind, to the system," he said.
Founder of advocacy group Nuclear for Australia Will Shackel said a "huge anti-nuclear disinformation push" at the last election harmed the public debate.
"We saw … a very sophisticated anti-nuclear campaign, which included elements of astroturfing, whether it was three-eyed fish, radioactive koalas, fearmongering about water and earthquakes," he said.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who presided over climate talks at COP31 in Türkiye, has previously ruled out nuclear as a "pipe dream", telling reporters in August his government was pursuing "practical, commonsense" renewables.

A now-lapsed parliamentary inquiry into nuclear power generation heard that setting up a nuclear industry in Australia would face substantial regulatory, workforce, supply-chain and construction hurdles.
Mr Gallagher said Australia's nuclear policy was a "travesty".
"We've run reactors continuously in Australia for over 50 years without any significant safety instances. There is no reason why we couldn't have a commercial power reactor system," he said.
"Australia is, unfortunately, going to be a price taker and not a leader in this space."
